title: XOM, CVX Are Already Up More Than 25% This Year — One Analyst Thinks There's Still More To Come For Big Oil - Stocktwits

The firm also noted that the company is entering a period of stronger organic cash flow growth as capital spending, excluding the Hess acquisition, continues to decline. Oil prices have been climbing amid the standoff between the U.S. and Iran as American forces attacked the Middle Eastern country for a 13th consecutive night on Thursday. Brent crude prices rose to over $100 a barrel before declining to about $98.90 at the time of writing. WTI crude was trading around $90.57. South Korea’s KOSPI declined 5.8% by Friday afternoon in Seoul, while Samsung and SK Hynix stocks slid 7.6% and 8.3%. The move in U.S. semiconductor stocks has become increasingly bundled with KOSPI, which is heavily weighted toward chipmakers Samsung and SK Hynix and has seen increased volatility lately. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU), a three-times leveraged ETF tracking South Korea’s largest stocks, dropped 8.5%. INTC was the top trending stock on Stocktwits early Friday, with retail sentiment moving to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘neutral’ the previous day. Retail traders debated the company’s capital expenditure plans and foundry business update, while analysts noted that Wall Street had largely expected a strong quarter, with much of the optimism already priced into the stock ahead of the earnings release. “INTC no way intel will stay at 100 and plus with that higher capex announcement wall street gonna dump on us,” a trader wrote, while another said, “$INTC can't hold a 9% gain for a few minutes, we're stuck here until 2027.” Intel plans to spend $20 billion this year, up from its previous forecast of $18 billion, and could tap the capital markets for funds. Tech giants Alphabet and Amazon recently raised enormous amounts through debt and equity despite having significant cash already. “INTC says they won't ramp Capex unless they were confident in customer commitments. Since they're raising Capex "significantly" next year, that means they're confident in those 10 long-term customers,” Deepwater Management founder Gene Munster said in an X post. Based on Intel’s fine print, Munster broadly believes that the AI infrastructure buildout is still in its early stages, with demand for its CPUs benefiting from the broader hyperscaler investment cycle. While he sees Intel as a beneficiary of the AI boom, he believes Nvidia and AMD remain better ways to invest in the trend, noting that much of Intel’s recent optimism is already reflected in its valuation. Intel’s turnaround is closely tied to its foundry business, which recently bagged new marquee customers such as Apple and Tesla. The unit narrowed its operating loss to $2.1 billion from a $3.2 billion loss a year earlier, but did not announce new customer wins in the report. The government-backed chipmaker’s second-quarter revenue increased 25% to $16.1 billion and adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.42 per share. Wall Street analysts had anticipated $14.5 billion in revenue and an adjusted profit of $0.22 per share, as per Fiscal.ai. The revenue expansion was largely driven by Intel’s data center operations, where sales soared 59% last quarter to $6.3 billion. "In data centers, the CPU is taking off," CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in an interview with Bloomberg. "Demand is outpacing our increasing supply, and so those are good problems to have." Intel’s third-quarter sales and profit forecasts also came in above expectations. As of the last close, INTC shares had declined 29% from their peak on June 22 but remain 172% higher year to date. title: XOM, CVX Stocks In Focus: Trump Criticizes Exxon And Chevron For Profiting From Iran-Driven Oil Price Surge — ‘They’re Making Too Much Money’ - Stocktwits
content: President Donald Trump criticized Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) on Monday, saying the oil giants made “too much money” as crude prices surged during the Iran war. He urged them to lower gasoline prices for consumers. Shares of Chevron were down 2.3% in afternoon trading, while Exxon Mobil was trading 0.8% lower. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “They’re making too much money based on a shortage. I don't like it,” according to CNBC. According to TheFly, Trump added, “I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger. You surprised I’m saying it? I’ll say it loud and clear. I’m not happy about it.” Trump also said, “Chevron, too much money. ExxonMobil, too much money. They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price,” CNBC reported. The remarks come as higher gasoline prices, driven by the Iran war, and broader cost-of-living concerns pose a political risk ahead of November’s midterm elections, when Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress. Trump also criticized Chevron Chief Executive Mike Wirth for not highlighting his administration’s pro-fossil fuel policies during an interview with Fox Business Network. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, “The only thing he conveniently forgot to mention ⁠is that, without the genius, foresight, strength, and stability, of the TRUMP Administration, the Oil Industry, and our Country itself, would be DEAD!" On the Fox Business interview, Wirth said Chevron was producing record amounts of oil in the U.S. and refining record volumes of crude. Trump also told oil companies to “get your consumer (retail!) Oil Prices DOWN, NOW!” Trump’s criticism comes days after Exxon Mobil and Chevron reported blockbuster second-quarter earnings as the Iran war pushed energy prices higher. Exxon Mobil’s quarterly profit more than doubled from a year earlier to $14.5 billion, its highest level since 2022, while Chevron posted record quarterly earnings of $12.1 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal. BlackRock (BLK) on Monday launched two tokenized money market funds, deepening its push into blockchain-based cash products for stablecoin issuers and crypto-native investors. The BlackRock Select Treasury Based Liquidity Fund (BSTBL) now has a tokenized share class issued on Ethereum (ETH), with BNY Mellon (BNY) as transfer agent and tokenization provider, the company stated. A second vehicle, the BlackRock Daily Reinvestment Stablecoin Reserve Vehicle (BRSRV), was launched,  with Securitize (SECZ) as transfer agent and tokenization provider, and intends to qualify as eligible reserve assets for permitted US payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. "As demand grows for high-quality reserve assets to support stablecoins and other tokenized financial products, these funds provide clients with additional choice in how they access and use money market fund investment solutions across traditional and digital markets,” said Jon Steel, Global Head of Product and Platform for BlackRock's Cash Management business. BlackRock first disclosed the products during its second-quarter earnings call last month, when Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Martin Small had said the filings were "about bringing BlackRock's core cash management capabilities to where digital assets clients are already operating." Small added that as stablecoins and digital wallets grow, "clients will need high-quality reserve and liquidity products that can operate natively in that digital ecosystem." The launch came after BlackRock’s BUIDL fund, its first tokenized money market offering, launched with Securitize in March 2024 and has since grown to around $2.5 billion in assets. BUIDL’s price continued trading at $1 during the past 24 hours. The retail sentiment around BUIDL remained in the ‘neutral’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘high’ levels over the past day. title: How a Hurricane Could Help Some Refineries—and Hurt Others - The Globe and Mail
content: Hurricane season in the United States can be a major driver of volatility in the energy sector, though investors tend to overlook nuances that can leave some companies heavily affected while others are barely scathed. When storms threaten the Gulf Coast, there is always a possibility of refinery closures, disruptions to production, infrastructure damage, and resulting increases in prices at the pump. Early October's Hurricane Isaias was a recent demonstration of how predicting the impacts of these events can be difficult. While forecasts initially called for Isaias to impact a wide area of Gulf Coast refineries, as landfall approached the projected impacted refinery capacity shrank considerably. For investors, the disruption to energy companies in the area may ultimately have been less than expected, but the lessons on how to seek opportunities remain. The impact of a hurricane on any specific company tends to come down to where its assets are located, how diversified its revenue streams are, and whether it can capture the widening crack spread that often occurs after refining capacity is reduced. As Isaias demonstrated, even if a hurricane doesn't do as much damage as initially anticipated, it can still cause bumpiness in the energy market. Companies may opt to reduce production or even shut down portions of their business preemptively. Investors were watching facilities like Chevron's (NYSE: CVX) in Mississippi, a major domestic refinery that faced potential flooding or outages as a result of the storm. While CVX shares remained flat from late September to Oct. 7, they quickly climbed as it became clear that Isaias would likely do less damage than originally expected. CVX is up about 4% in the last month. By contrast, shares of rival Phillips 66 (NYSE: PSX) have risen 14% in the last month, a sign of investor optimism in a company that was less likely from the beginning to be affected by Isaias' path. Phillips is a nuanced play in a scenario involving a Gulf Coast hurricane, given its diversified business lines. The company has refining, midstream, chemicals, and other businesses, some of which are significantly more exposed to risk from a hurricane than others. While PSX shares are up an impressive 125% year to date (YTD), this performance largely reflects the crack spread expansion that has benefited refiners broadly amid the ongoing Iran conflict rather than a specific response to Isaias or other weather events. Phillips' midstream business is critical because it provides cash flow that is based primarily on fees, not on the price of crude—and this may make PSX more stable in the case of future hurricanes. Aside from Chevron's Mississippi assets, the company's deepwater Gulf of Mexico operations also face the risk of temporary shutdowns during severe storms in the area. This has the potential to impact not only the company's refining operations but also its crude production volumes. Still, with crude as costly as it is, the impact to the company's revenue from a brief production interruption is less damaging—and indeed a crude price spike following a hurricane, as in the case of Isaias, helps to reduce that damage further. The VanEck Oil Refiners ETF (NYSEARCA: CRAK) is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds a basket of global oil refiner stocks, with domestic names making up just 35% of the portfolio. Even if those stocks are impacted by a North American hurricane, the bulk of the portfolio will be unaffected. At the same time, virtually all of the companies in CRAK's collection will benefit from a tighter global refined market caused by U.S. Gulf Coast disruption. Potential setbacks for domestic refiners may mean a boon for international rivals. CRAK's net assets have surged dramatically this year as investors have capitalized on wide crack spreads and rapid share price increases in refiners. The fund has year-to-date returns of about 80%, which makes its fairly high expense ratio of 0.61% much more tolerable. Not all of the current tailwinds—limited supply due to the Iran war, elevated crack spreads, and Gulf Coast capacity reduction—may continue over the long term. Crack spreads tend to normalize within a few weeks of a U.S. hurricane, so investors new to CRAK should keep in mind that they may be buying after the Iran war has delivered significant returns and as hurricane season nears its end for the year. title: Chevron vs. ExxonMobil: Which Energy Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - The Motley Fool
content: ExxonMobil's 8.9% net margin outpaces Chevron's 6.7%, but Chevron's Guyana expansion could reshape the competitive landscape. Energy markets remain volatile in 2026, leaving many investors wondering which industry titan offers greater stability. Choosing between Chevron (CVX -1.23%) and ExxonMobil (XOM -1.32%) requires a look at their efficiency and growth trajectories. Chevron focuses on expanding its footprint through major acquisitions, while ExxonMobil leverages its massive global scale to maintain industry-leading profitability. Both companies are primary players in the fossil fuel landscape, yet they approach resource management and capital allocation differently. Comparing their financials and risks reveals which stock might fit your portfolio better. In its latest annual report, filed for the most recent fiscal year, Chevron details its strategy among renewable energy stocks and oil producers. It has significantly expanded its reach through the July 2025 acquisition of Hess, which included a 30 percent interest in the Stabroek Block in Guyana. The company also maintains significant contractual obligations for natural gas and crude oil, partnering with entities such as Hess Midstream (HESM -0.10%) for midstream services. In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $184.4 billion, a decline of roughly 4.6% from the previous year. This revenue drop contributed to a net income of approximately $12.3 billion for the period. The company reported a net margin of nearly 6.7%, which measures how much profit a firm retains for every dollar of sales. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.2x, meaning the company uses very little total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 1.2x, indicating $1.20 in current assets for every $1.00 in current liabilities. Free cash flow for the period was roughly $16.6 billion, representing the cash remaining after the business pays for its capital expenditures. In its latest annual report, ExxonMobil is positioned as a global energy and petrochemical leader producing oil, natural gas, and chemical products. It serves markets worldwide, backed by a massive workforce and a diverse portfolio of refined products and lubricants. While the company does not disclose specific major customer concentrations in its filings, its massive scale allows it to maintain a dominant position across the energy supply chain. During FY 2025, the company reported revenue of approximately $323.9 billion, down nearly 4.5% year over year. Despite the lower top line, it achieved a net income of roughly $28.8 billion. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 8.9%, which reflects the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses and taxes are paid. According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.2x, suggesting a conservative approach to borrowing relative to shareholders' equity. The company also maintains a current ratio of roughly 1.2x, which measures its ability to cover short-term debts with assets that can be quickly converted to cash. Free cash flow reached nearly $23.6 billion, providing significant capital for dividends or reinvestment, which is a key differentiator in the integrated oil and gas industry. Chevron faces significant risks from commodity price volatility, which can lead to asset impairments if oil prices drop sharply. Operational hazards, such as hurricanes and geopolitical conflicts in regions like the Middle East, can also force production suspensions. Furthermore, the company must manage integration risks following its 2025 acquisition of Hess, as well as ongoing climate-related litigation in federal courts. ExxonMobil operates in a highly competitive environment and faces pressure from shifting global energy demands and stricter environmental regulations. It competes with other international giants for limited resource rights and market share across every continent. Like its peers, the company is vulnerable to price fluctuations in the global crude oil and natural gas markets, which directly impact its profitability. Chevron carries a slightly lower Forward P/E, while ExxonMobil offers a slightly lower P/S ratio, which measures market capitalization against sales over the past twelve months. When comparing Chevron and ExxonMobil, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock. First off, there's profitability and growth. As it turns out, the two companies have very similar margins. ExxonMobil's five-year average operating margin is 12.7%, and Chevron's is 12.4%. Similarly, ExxonMobil's year-over-year revenue growth has averaged 12.3% since 2022, while Chevron's is 14.4%. All in all, there's not much to separate these two stocks in terms of growth and profitability. Another factor to consider is each stock's valuation. Again, the differences between the two stocks are slight. Their P/S ratios are nearly identical at 2.1x and 2.0x. However, on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) basis, Chevron is slightly more affordable at 12.9x versus 13.9x for ExxonMobil. Last, there's income potential. Chevron has a current dividend yield of 3.27%, while ExxonMobil has a dividend yield of 2.37%. That may give Chevron a leg up for income-seeking investors. To sum up, Chevron and ExxonMobil are very similar stocks. ExxonMobil has been slightly more profitable over the last five years, while Chevron has grown somewhat faster, is slightly more affordable, and offers a larger dividend yield. title: Venezuela's Oil Revival Is Gaining Momentum—3 Energy Stocks Positioned to Benefit - MarketBeat
content:
Disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have sent energy prices soaring this year, contributing to record-high diesel prices and higher costs at the pump for American consumers. As the United States looks to offset lost Middle Eastern supply, attention is shifting to Venezuela, home to more than 17% of the world's proven crude oil reserves. Following January's Operation Absolute Resolve, efforts to revive Venezuela's oil industry have gained momentum. On Aug. 31, the White House announced an agreement with North American Blue Energy Partners outlining up to $100 billion in potential investments to develop 17 oil fields containing approximately 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. But the U.S. government isn’t alone in that effort. Oil giants Chevron NYSE: CVX, BP NYSE: BP, and Halliburton NYSE: HAL are making high-stakes, multi-billion-dollar investments in Venezuela, targeting the country’s massive crude oil reserves, which at around 330 billion gallons are the largest on Earth. In September, Houston-based Chevron announced a plan to invest $7 billion over five years in its Venezuelan joint ventures. Ultimately, the integrated oil and gas company will be targeting 600,000 barrels per day in production, or more than double its current total. Importantly, Chevron estimates its production costs will come in at less than $20 per barrel. For context, Brent crude—the global oil benchmark—is around $105 per barrel, down more than 15% from its one-year high but up more than 80% from its pre-war and one-year low in December 2025. In Q2, Chevron produced around 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (a measure that includes both oil and natural gas production). If the company is able to scale to an additional 300,000 gallons per day of Venezuelan production, that additional output would account for approximately 7% of total company-wide output. Venezuela’s political environment remains delicate. But if the country can maintain stability, Chevron’s plan is a bullish signal to energy investors following a Q2 that saw adjusted earnings of $12 billion, or $6.06 per share, and $15.4 billion in adjusted free cash flow. Chevron currently carries a Moderate Buy rating, with 22 of 28 analysts covering the stock assigning it a Buy rating. The analyst consensus price target implies around 2% downside, but the company’s dividend—which it has raised for 38 consecutive years and currently yields around 3.3%—pays shareholders to be patient. Chevron is scheduled to report Q3 earnings on Oct. 30. In August, BP and the Venezuelan government signed agreements to advance offshore gas development, building on an initial memorandum of understanding signed in April. As part of the deal, BP received an exploration and production license for Phase 2 of the Loran field in the Plataforma Deltana area, which contains an estimated 4 trillion cubic feet of recoverable natural gas resources. While BP has not disclosed a dollar amount for its investment, the production license granted for Loran Phase 2—a massive and untapped resource. The opportunity comes on the heels of BP's strong Q2 results. The company reported revenue of $69.11 billion, up 106.1% year over year and ahead of analysts' consensus estimate of $57.89 billion. Analysts have assigned BP a consensus Moderate Buy rating, with 17 of 27 analysts covering the stock marking it as a Buy. As an oilfield services provider, Houston-based Halliburton strives to play an integral role in the revival of Venezuela’s oil infrastructure. On Sept. 21, Halliburton announced strategic memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with Brazil-based Eneva and WESCA, a Venezuelan engineering, construction, and oil and gas operator with more than 40 years of experience. The agreements aim to support Halliburton's reentry into Venezuela's energy sector, including field evaluation, development planning, and the use of digital technologies to assess underground oil and gas reservoirs. This is a major catalyst. Halliburton is positioning itself to leverage existing local ties and equipment to generate revenue by repairing aging infrastructure before companies like Chevron and BP can ramp up production. The news comes on the back of Halliburton posting its fourth consecutive quarterly earnings beat in Q2. Revenue of $5.7 billion also beat analysts’ consensus forecast, while the adjusted operating margin reached 12% and free cash flow registered $668 million. The company also repurchased approximately $200 million worth of its shares.HAL carries an analyst consensus rating of Moderate Buy, with 18 of the 25 analysts currently covering the stock assigning it a Buy rating. The near-term story centers on the company's readiness to present its latest quarterly results. Setting a date for the call has nudged the stock into a window where market participants sift through every clue about how the business performed across a stretch of swinging crude. Pre-results periods often bring heightened attention, as the market tries to read whether the major stood its ground. What tends to draw the closest watch is the mix of upstream realizations, refining margins and cash generation. In a soft crude setting, the strength of the downstream and gas arms can take on added importance, since they do not move in lockstep with the price of raw crude. A large slice of the growth story runs through the Permian Basin, the prolific shale region straddling the American Southwest. The company has built a sizable footprint there, and steady output from low-cost acreage has become a key driver of its upstream plans. These barrels tend to be cheap to lift, which helps the business stay resilient when crude drifts lower. Management has framed the Permian around disciplined growth rather than all-out expansion, steering capital toward the most productive acreage while keeping spending in check. That measured approach has become a hallmark of how the major describes its upstream engine, and it feeds into the broader theme of capital discipline that runs across the whole sector. Beyond American shale, the company runs a sprawling international portfolio spanning offshore developments, legacy fields and a growing liquefied natural gas business. Gas has become an ever more important thread, as power grids around the world lean on the cleaner-burning fuel to balance the swing toward renewables. The company ships gas to markets across Asia and Europe, tying it to durable global demand. This international reach gives the business a spread of revenue streams that do not all rise and fall together. Projects in different regions carry their own rhythms, and the gas arm in particular ties the company to long-term supply arrangements that lend some steadiness. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. On the downstream side, the company operates refineries and a products network that turn crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and lubricants sold across many markets. This arm gives the business a revenue stream that can move counter to the crude price, because cheaper feedstock can widen the spread between raw crude and finished fuels. That counterbalance is part of the appeal of the integrated model. When upstream realizations soften, the downstream arm can sometimes take up the slack, smoothing the overall mix. Scale and integration give the downstream arm an added edge. Stepping back, the wider field of US Oil and Gas Stocks has been shaped by swinging prices, careful supply moves from OPEC+ and an ongoing conversation about the energy transition. American producers have leaned heavily on capital discipline, resisting the urge to flood the market with new barrels, and that restraint has colored how the whole complex trades through choppy stretches. Within that picture, the largest integrated majors command the most attention because of their scale and their staying power through downturns. The company sits firmly in that top tier, and its quarterly results tend to be read as a signal for how the broader American energy space is faring at any given moment. Sentiment across the complex has swung with the crude tape, and the long debate over the energy transition has added a layer of uncertainty to the horizon. A central force shaping the sector has been the supply stance of OPEC+. The alliance of major exporters has been managing how much crude reaches the market, and every adjustment ripples through global benchmarks. When the group signals more barrels, prices often ease; when it pulls back, the market can firm. That push and pull has kept crude in a choppy band through much of the current year. For a major of this size, these swings matter but do not set the entire course. title: Why Are BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, USO, UCO Stocks Rising Overnight? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of multiple oil companies and oil exchange-traded funds climbed overnight late Sunday after Brent crude prices rose above $90 a barrel amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted on X late Sunday, “Responding to this weekend's US-Iran escalation, Brent crude is currently above $90 a barrel in Asian trading.” WTI crude futures expiring in August also rose more than 2% to $84.33 per barrel. As a result, oil companies Battalion Oil Corp. (BATL) and Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) rose more than 7% and by over 8% in the overnight session. Oil majors Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) also rose about 1% each. Meanwhile, the United States Oil Fund (USO), which tracks the daily price movements of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), climbed more than 2% at the time of writing, while ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil (UCO) rallied more than 3%. The Light, Sweet Crude Oil Futures (CL_F) were also 2% higher. Oil prices soared back up as tensions between the U.S. and Iran escalated over the weekend after the American military launched a ninth consecutive night of attacks on the Middle Eastern country. “CENTCOM began conducting a new wave of strikes against Iran at 7 p.m. ET today for the ninth consecutive night. The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. Over the weekend, CENTCOM confirmed that a third U.S. service member had died following recent fighting in the Middle East. The military had initially reported two fatalities and one service member missing after an Iranian attack in Jordan on July 17 before later confirming the third death. Meanwhile, Iran Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi condemned the U.S. strike on the under-construction Darquoin power plant, calling it a dangerous attack on Iran's civilian infrastructure. In a post on X, he said the strike made Washington fully responsible for the resulting instability and warned that Iran would take appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and interests. "The longer the Strait remains closed and the war escalates the greater ​the risk that oil prices will have to rise to around $150/barrel to bring demand down to match the hit to supply," Shane Oliver, Head of Investment Strategy and Chief Economist, at AMP reportedly told Reuters, adding that "This is not our base case but it's a high risk again." Meanwhile, Garfield Reynolds, MLIV Asia team leader at Bloomberg, reportedly said the widening spread between Brent crude and WTI reflects growing concerns that an escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict could disrupt global energy supplies, though the gap remains narrow enough that equity markets have largely shrugged off the risk compared with the early stages of the war. Analyst Patrick De Haan said on X that rising oil prices would likely send gas prices higher in the U.S. in the coming week. “Brent crude oil up ~3% reaching $90/bbl, while WTI crude up ~2% to nearly $85/bbl. RBOB up 5c/gal, national average gas price will hit $4/gal either tomorrow or Tuesday, likely to see increases ahead for most states!” he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BATL stock slipped from ‘extremely bullish’ to ‘bullish’ over 24 hours while it was in the ‘neutral’ territory for TPET. XOM and CVX stocks were trending in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing. Sentiment for USO and UCO stocks, meanwhile, was in the ‘extremely bullish’ and ‘bearish’ territories, respectively. One bullish user on Stocktwits said, “$USO $BATL I'm not selling, no matter what." BATL stock is up more than 46% this year, while TPET has declined nearly 60% in the same time. XOM and CVX have gained more than 20% each in 2026. USO and UCO have surged nearly 80% and 113% year-to-date. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Advanced Micro Devices appears to have secured, or is close to securing, Claude developer Anthropic as a chip customer, with speculation swirling online after a senior executive referenced the AI startup in code published on GitHub. AMD shares rose 1.3% in the overnight session late Sunday. A YAML code file from an unnamed AMD senior director listed Anthropic as a “customer,” chip news site SemiAnalysis reported on Sunday. SemiAnalysis said Anthropic was assigned the maximum 30 “priority boost points,” placing it alongside existing hyperscale customers such as Meta – fueling speculation that AMD could formally announce a partnership with the AI startup at its flagship Advancing AI conference next week. “Note that Anthropic is still in the evaluation phase, and if AMD doesn’t announce Anthropic at its upcoming Advancing AI conference, that means @AnushElangovan’s FDE team has yet to address all of Anthropic’s concerns regarding software quality, and further improvement will be needed,” SemiAnalysis wrote. Meanwhile, Anthropic has reportedly been hiring engineers with ROCm experience (AMD’s AI software stack), suggesting it is preparing to further diversify its computing infrastructure, Jefferies analyst Blayne Curtis said in a recent note. Anthropic is not a publicly confirmed AMD customer. The AI startup has publicly said it trains and serves Claude using a mix of Nvidia GPUs, Amazon’s Trainium chips, and Google’s TPUs, with Amazon remaining its primary cloud and training partner. The AMD Advancing AI 2026 conference will run over Wednesday and Thursday at the Moscone Center in San Francisco. The company is expected to focus its announcements around AI infrastructure, new silicon-to-software pipelines, and enterprise-tier development. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AMD remained ‘bullish,’ unchanged from the previous day, with traders noting speculation that Anthropic is becoming an AMD customer. “The recent market bloodbath just flushed $AMD from its 584 peak to the 490s. Daily RSI is screaming deep oversold in the 29-34 range. This is exactly what an extreme discount looks like,” a trader wrote. “The massive ‘Advancing AI’ event drops July 22-23 with the 2nm Zen 6 and Helios platform. This killer catalyst will likely torch the shorts, triggering a violent rebound off the $478 hard support next week,” they said. AMD stock has declined for three days straight, losing 16%, but remains 132% higher year to date. The chipmaker will report its second-quarter results on Aug. 4. SemiAnalysis said an unnamed AMD senior director posted it, not Vice President Anush Elangovan. AtaiBeckley (ATAI), Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and Travelers Companies (TRV), all reached 52-week highs on Friday as investors moved away from vulnerable areas of the technology sector and toward companies backed by stronger fundamentals, with capital flowing into businesses with clearer growth catalysts, essential services and proven earnings power. Atai Life Sciences and Palo Alto Networks stocks ended the session 0.9% and 1% higher, while Travelers Companies stock climbed 9%. AtaiBeckley stock reached a four-year high of $7.22 on Friday, as its psychedelic medicine business gained momentum after a multibillion-dollar acquisition agreement reshaped investor expectations for the sector. The rally followed Eli Lilly and Co. (LLY )'s July 16 announcement of a deal to acquire AtaiBeckley for $6.75 per share in upfront cash, valued at up to $3.8 billion, including milestone-based payments. The transaction pushed psychedelic treatments closer to mainstream pharmaceutical acceptance as investors viewed the acquisition as a sign of confidence from a major drugmaker. The deal centers on AtaiBeckley’s experimental therapies, including BPL-003 and VLS-01. BPL-003, an intranasal formulation based on 5-MeO-DMT, is being developed for treatment-resistant depression and has received FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Palo Alto Networks stock touched a record high of $368.80 as investors showed confidence in its cybersecurity business. Demand increased for Palo Alto’s security platforms, including Cortex and XSIAM, as companies prioritized protecting their digital systems from growing AI threats. Capital One upgraded the stock to “Overweight” from “Equalweight” and increased its price target to $421 from $307. The firm expects the cybersecurity company to benefit from growing demand for AI infrastructure, rising cyber threats, a spike in security spending and the need to protect new AI systems. Retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘bearish’ territory. The Travelers Companies stock also reached a record high of $370.43 after reporting stronger-than-expected fiscal second-quarter results. The insurer posted earnings of $10.04 per share, while revenue reached $12.15 billion, both exceeding the analysts’ consensus estimates of $5.39 and $10.98 billion, respectively, according to Fiscal AI data. Travelers improved its combined ratio to 83.6% from 90.3% last year, showing stronger underwriting performance. Investor sentiment toward the stock remained positive. So far this year, TRV, ATAI, and PANW stocks have gained between 26% and 94%. (ORCL) and SpaceX (SPCX) fell to annual lows last week amid concerns around future growth, mounting debt, and a post-IPO profit-taking scenario. NFLX stock fell more than 7% at close on Friday as investors continued to react negatively to the company’s latest earnings outlook. ORCL declined to a 52-week low before reversing to close up 1.77%. SPCX stock extended two consecutive weeks of losses to close down more than 5%. NFLX stock fell to a yearly low of $65.08, about 45% down from its 12-month high, as the streaming giant’s weaker-than-expected outlook for the third quarter deepened investor concerns about its future growth. The company forecast third-quarter earnings of $0.82 per share on $12.86 billion in revenue, slightly below analysts' expectations. However, during the earnings call, CFO Spencer Neumann said quarterly growth may appear uneven due to tougher comparisons with last year, stressing that Netflix remains focused on full-year performance. He expects third-quarter revenue to rise about 12%, driven by subscriber growth, selective price hikes and expanding advertising revenue. Netflix also narrowed its 2026 revenue guidance to $51 billion to $51.4 billion. Meanwhile, veteran investor Michael Burry said last week that he is on the fence about whether Netflix produces content “that is long-lasting, watchable on repeat, across generations.” Drawing comparisons with peers Disney and Pixar, he said the rivals “produce evergreen content,” raising questions about whether Netflix’s content can generate similar long-term value. NFLX stock is down more than 24% this year even as retail sentiment remains ‘extremely bullish’ on Stocktwits. ORCL stock fell to a 52-week low of $121.50 on Friday, although the company’s shares recovered to close in the green. Oracle has been on the receiving end of criticism for its aggressive spending on cloud infrastructure and rapidly growing debt. The company recently said that it plans to spend up to $95 billion in capital expenditures in fiscal 2027 and raise $40 billion through debt and equity. This has fueled worries about rising leverage and negative free cash flow. Those concerns intensified after S&P Global downgraded Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, citing its reliance on a handful of large customers, including OpenAI. The company has also been weighed down by growing uncertainty around OpenAI's business prospects, raising questions about Oracle's AI-driven growth strategy. ORCL stock is down more than 35% this year. Despite the worries, retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘extremely bullish’ at the time of writing as users see the dip as an opportunity. SPCX stock fell to an all-time low of $122.12, dipping further below its IPO price of $135. Elon Musk’s aerospace company, which made its historic debut on Wall Street last month, declined for a sixth-straight session. SpaceX has seen heavy selling following its aggressive capital-raising plans. Meanwhile, last week the company scrubbed the latest launch of its Starship mega rocket due to technical glitches. Musk said in a post on X that the launch was automatically aborted after some of the engines failed to ignite. In a separate post, he said SpaceX plans to replace two Raptor engines before making another launch attempt, which is most likely to take place early next week. The test flight was intended to mark the debut of an upgraded version of Starship designed to support future Starlink deployments and NASA's lunar missions. According to a Reuters report, SpaceX is now targeting July 23 for its next launch attempt. SPCX stock is down nearly 23% since its debut, with retail sentiment on Stocktwits ‘bearish’ at the time of writing. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) jumped 3% overnight late Monday as retail traders bet that the final acute myeloid leukemia (AML) readout could turn this week’s Fox appearance into a launchpad for Big Pharma interest. SLS stock surged 12% on Friday to close at $13.19, capping a 3% weekly gain. The speculation is related to Sellas’ Phase 3 Regal trial of galinpepimut-S (GPS) in AML. The study is nearing the 80th event required to trigger its final analysis. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits sllipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a week ago amid a 12% rise in 24-hour message volumes. However, watchers for the stock have risen nearly 5% in a month. One trader called CEO Angelos Stergiou’s media strategy a “masterclass in forcing a Big Pharma decision,” saying that the period between the 80th event and topline data could trap short sellers. “We aren't waiting for a buyout—we’re manufacturing the conditions that make a bidding war inevitable,” the user said. Another investor expects Sellas to announce the topline results around Stergiou’s Fox appearance, while projecting a surge in the stock and a bidding war.  A third user said Stergiou had spent more than five years protecting Regal and would not risk the program for “30 minutes of television fame,” adding: “The timeline is compressed because the destination is set.” Other traders predicted that Stergiou would discuss the company’s two flagship drugs and the path to topline data. Several named Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Pfizer, AbbVie, Eli Lilly, and Bristol Myers as possible bidders. “One thing is for sure, JnJ will be watching Fox News,” another user said, citing LinkedIn activity. Stergiou said on LinkedIn last week that he would return to Fox & Friends after a recent discussion with host Brian Kilmeade about the future of AI-powered cancer vaccines. He said that the segment’s date and time were still being finalized, adding that the discussion would cover Sellas’ clinical programs and efforts to advance more personalized cancer care through GPS and SLS009 (the company’s second clinical-stage drug candidate). Meanwhile, retail takeover speculation has intensified as the market value swelled from about $73 million at the start of 2024 to more than $1.5 billion by mid-2026, with Regal nearing completion. Investors have pointed to Stergiou’s previous references to “strategic partners,” changes to executive change-of-control benefits and the potential commercial value of GPS and SLS009 (the second drug). Regal is a Phase 3 study evaluating GPS in AML patients who have entered a second complete remission. The trial had reached 78 of the 80 events required to trigger its final analysis. Sellas has said that the study would be considered successful if GPS extends median overall survival to 12.6 months, compared with eight months for best available therapy. Stergiou previously said the company would announce the 80th event and then enter a formal quiet period until topline results are available. He has also pushed back against claims that the slower event rate necessarily means patients in the control arm are surviving longer. Since Sellas remains blinded, neither the company nor investors know which arm is responsible for the slower accumulation of events. The CEO has also rejected calls to stop the trial at 78 events, saying, “Events are our statistical currency,” and warning that an early halt could create regulatory concerns and timing bias. The company operates a sizable position in the Permian Basin of West Texas and New Mexico, where low operating costs and short cycle times let crews flex activity as the market shifts. Chevron is a fully integrated powerhouse, managing everything from oil wells to gas stations. The company is also growing its presence in renewable energy stocks to diversify its long-term portfolio as it integrates its acquisition of Hess. Occidental Petroleum focuses primarily on oil and gas exploration and production in the United States and the Middle East. That gives Occidental an edge in profitability, although Chevron is much larger, with a total net income of $21 billion, far higher than Occidental's $4.3 billion. Another factor to consider is each company's valuation. Here, again, Occidental can claim a slight edge. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 9.4x is less than Chevron's 12.7x. Earlier this month, Chevron (NYSE:CVX) agreed to take a one-time loss of roughly $3 billion to $4 billion. That sounds like an odd move for a company coming off a blowout quarter. Then again, the timing may be the whole point. Chevron is one of the world's largest integrated oil companies. It pumps crude and natural gas (the upstream business), then refines it into gasoline and diesel sold at stations many drivers pass every day. When oil and fuel prices jump, both halves can cash in at once. That's what happened in the second quarter. For investors evaluating top sector opportunities among the 10 Most Promising Energy Stocks to Buy Now, the harder question is what Chevron looks like once that windfall cools, and the answer depends less on oil prices than on how much of the company's progress it actually controls. The headline numbers were staggering. Adjusted earnings per share hit $6.06 in fiscal Q2 2026, up from $1.41 in Q1 and $1.77 a year earlier. Free cash flow reached $18.1 billion, and Chevron used it to cut total debt by a record $8.4 billion in a single quarter. Price wasn't the only driver, though. Production climbed to 4,070 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 20% from a year earlier, largely thanks to the former Hess assets and growth in the Permian Basin and the Gulf of America. US refineries ran a record 1.07 million barrels per day at utilization above 97%. That operational muscle is Chevron's real edge. Scale spreads costs across a huge production base, and owning refineries cushions the blow when crude prices and fuel margins move in different directions. The more telling evidence is what Chevron is fixing on its own. It has reached $3 billion in annual run-rate structural cost cuts since 2024, within a program targeting $3 billion to $4 billion by the end of 2026. Hess-related synergies hit $1.5 billion a year, 50% above the original goal. The Hess Midstream deal fits that pattern. Chevron will hand its stake and general partner position to Hess Midstream for $200 million in cash plus restructured contracts, and it expects Bakken unit midstream costs to fall by about 50%. The loss exists because those future savings can't be booked as an asset, and Chevron plans to treat it as a special item. The deal also moves roughly $3.7 billion of Hess Midstream debt off its books. Chevron is planting seeds for later, too. A 20-year deal to supply Microsoft with about 2.67 gigawatts of power for a West Texas data center puts it among the energy companies chasing AI power demand. To read more, see our 10 Best AI Energy Stocks to Buy in 2026. Here's the catch. Earnings per share are expected to fall 13.47% in 2027, which suggests the market treats the recent quarter as closer to a peak than a new baseline. The first half of the year shows how fast things swing. Chevron's international downstream business lost $1,013 million in Q1, then earned $2,457 million in Q2. Free cash flow went from negative $1.5 billion to positive $18.1 billion in three months. A business that moves that much with commodity prices can't promise smooth growth; a cycle rival Occidental Petroleum can't escape either. Self-help softens that blow, but it can't offset a sharp oil slide alone. At 12.35 times forward earnings, as of October 9, Chevron trades almost exactly in line with the sector's 12.30 and below its own five-year average of 13.86. On the surface, that looks like a mild discount. The asterisk is the earnings path. A forward multiple can make a stock look cheaper than it is when profits are expected to shrink 13.47% the following year. So the gap to the five-year average is a weaker bargain signal than it first appears. What tips the scale back is the balance sheet. A net debt ratio of 13.1% after the record paydown gives Chevron room to keep funding its $1.78 quarterly dividend and buybacks through a softer stretch. In Q2 alone, it paid $3,504 million in dividends and repurchased $3,117 million of stock, which keeps it in the conversation alongside elite income compounders featured among the Top 11 Dividend Kings to Buy for Safe Dividend Growth. Hedge funds trimmed their exposure slightly, with 101 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, down from 103 in the prior one. Short interest sits at 1.06% of the float, a sign of relatively limited bearish positioning. Chevron's valuation doesn't look stretched, but it isn't a deep bargain once the expected earnings dip is factored in. What separates it from a pure oil-price bet is the self-help: lower costs, less debt, and a cheaper Bakken operation, all of which should hold even if prices cool. That makes the setup a better fit for patient, income-focused investors than for anyone counting on another quarter like the last one. If the cost program stalls, or debt starts creeping back up as earnings fall, the case gets much weaker. After a stretch in which the alliance had been gradually restoring barrels it had earlier withheld, the choice to stand pat signaled a more cautious approach to balancing global demand against available supply. For the integrated majors, that kind of restraint tends to put a floor under prices during soft patches, helping crude settle into a narrower band rather than sliding lower. News of the supply pause spread quickly as trading opened, and energy names featured prominently in coverage of the day's commodity and corporate headlines. Market participants spent the session weighing what a steadier crude band might mean for the largest producers, and the integrated structure of this company placed it near the center of that conversation. The broader mood across the market was constructive, with sentiment buoyed by easing trade tensions after softer signals on tariffs, and that backdrop gave the energy story room to resonate. What distinguishes this company within the sector is the span of its operations, which reach from the wellhead through to the finished product. On the upstream side, the group explores for and produces crude and natural gas across a wide geographic footprint. Downstream, it refines those raw materials into fuels and lubricants, while its chemicals interests convert hydrocarbons into materials used across manufacturing. The production arm of the company reaches across continents, from long-established basins to newer developments that have reshaped its output in recent years. A prominent strand of that effort has been its expanding presence in low-cost onshore acreage and in high-quality offshore developments, where the group has concentrated drilling where barrels can be produced efficiently. That emphasis on advantaged resources reflects a wider theme across the sector, in which the largest producers prioritize the most cost-effective barrels in their portfolios. Readers following Oil and Gas Stocks can place this update within its wider category. The refining operation anchors the company's downstream presence, turning crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and a range of other products that move through the global economy. Refining margins depend on the gap between the cost of crude feedstock and the price of finished fuels, a spread that can widen when raw-material costs ease. In a range-bound crude environment, that dynamic can give the downstream arm a steadier footing, helping to balance the contribution from the rest of the enterprise. Alongside crude, natural gas has grown into an increasingly important part of the energy conversation, and the company carries a meaningful presence across gas production and the chilled, liquefied form that moves across oceans. Demand for cleaner-burning fuel has supported interest in gas as economies weigh how to balance reliability against lower emissions, and the largest majors have been expanding their footprint in this corner of the market. The gradual shift in the global energy mix adds another dimension to how the enterprise is framed. A range-bound crude market places particular emphasis on how capital is managed. Rather than ramping spending aggressively in response to every price move, the largest integrated majors have leaned toward steadiness, directing capital to their most advantaged projects while keeping a firm grip on costs. That measured approach is designed to let the enterprise generate cash across a variety of price conditions rather than depending on a sustained commodity rally. The group belongs to a small circle of large companies that have lifted their payout year after year across many decades, a track record that has made it a fixture among dependable payers and a frequent reference point in discussions of durable cash generation. That heritage is part of why a steadier crude backdrop draws attention, since calmer conditions tend to support the cash engine that underpins the distribution.
